questions.q: What geometric pattern did Harappan streets follow?
questions.a: The streets followed a grid pattern, crossing each other at right angles. A wrong answer suggests the student is confusing ancient cities with natural, unplanned settlements that grew organically over time.

questions.q: Why do historians believe Harappan cities were planned before they were built?
questions.a: Because the city was divided into orderly rectangular blocks by straight streets, which is impossible to achieve if a city grows haphazardly. A wrong answer shows the student failed to link the "grid" design to the idea of "intentional planning."

questions.q: If you were to design a city today like the Harappans, how would you arrange your streets?
questions.a: I would draw straight, parallel lines in one direction and cross them with perpendicular lines to form squares. This shows the student can apply the grid concept to a new scenario rather than just memorizing a definition.

questions.q: How does the size of the streets in Harappan cities help us understand their daily life?
questions.a: The streets were wide enough for carts to pass, indicating that trade and transport of goods were important parts of city life. A wrong answer suggests the student is not connecting physical architecture to social or economic function.

questions.q: Could a city be "planned" if all its houses were different sizes and shapes?
questions.a: It would be harder to call it planned, as the Harappan use of standardized bricks ensured uniformity and order. A wrong answer shows the student doesn't understand that "standardization" is a key marker of organized, planned societies.

questions.q: Design a simple map of a town using the Harappan "grid" style; what would be at the corners of your blocks?
questions.a: The map should show straight, crossing lines with clearly defined rectangular areas for houses or buildings. An answer that shows winding, random paths reveals a failure to internalize the grid concept.
